reason: Attack failed, and it failed by one word, which is the interesting part. THE TRAP. The Virginia Woolf Society of Great Britain keeps a Misquotations and Misattributions page, and this sentence is on it. What is listed there as false is "One cannot EAT well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well", and the society gives the genuine Woolf sentence as the one with "think well". That single verb is the whole difference between a real citation and a card that would have gone out under a flagged misquotation, and the verifier shipped "think well". It cleared the trap. I would have refuted on it without hesitation had it read "eat". THE TEXT. I downloaded the Project Gutenberg of Australia file 0200791 whole (212 KB) and searched it. The sentence is at line 541, reading "One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well." Character for character the proposal, commas included. I then counted the divisions in the file rather than trusting the chapter claim: the section headings are bare words, ONE at line 60, TWO at 728, THREE at 1209, FOUR at 1692, FIVE at 2338, SIX at 2800, so line 541 falls inside ONE and "chapter 1" is right. The locator's description is accurate too: the sentence follows immediately on "The human frame being what it is, heart, body and brain all mixed together... a good dinner is of great importance to good talk", and the scene is the Fernham dinner, with the beef and prunes in the next sentence. Independent corroboration of both chapter and wording from the Woolf Society entry above. I looked hard for transcription drift in this witness and found the one risk named in its own production notes: "Italics in the book have been converted to upper case." That is real, and visible a line later where PROBABLY and HOPE are shouting. But the shipped sentence contains no italics in Woolf and none in the transcription, so the alteration does not touch it. Source line is 52 characters, leads with the author's name, no dash, and its apostrophe in One's is the curly one. Tag Essay is the form of the work. Theme: better than it looks at a glance. Read as a standalone aphorism it is a remark about dinner, but the paragraph it sits in is Woolf deciding whether she may say "The dinner was not good" to her host and concluding she may not, and then saying the plain thing about the human frame anyway. That is June's blurb almost literally, so the fit is earned and not just charming. TWO NON-FATAL REMARKS. (1) The evidence field calls Project Gutenberg of Australia 0200791 an "edition", which flatters it: its header says only "Edition: 1", names Col Choat as producer, and states no copy-text, so it is a transcription of unknown descent rather than a named edition. The wording is confirmed by a second, unrelated authority, so the line is safe, but the evidence should say transcription and should cite the Woolf Society alongside it rather than resting on one file. Secondary sources place the sentence at page 18, which I did not verify against a scan and so am not proposing for the source line. (2) MONTH COLLISION. My read, offered not asserted: the Mrs Dalloway line is the more famous but says nothing about the month's subject, while this one comes out of a passage about what politeness stops you saying, so this is the June line and Mrs Dalloway should wait.
